messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Kumar had always been a stoic man, but the year his granddaughter spent in and out of hospitals with leukemia had shaken him to his core. The smell of antiseptic and hospital corridors still brought back the memories like a tidal wave crashing against the shore. Just last week, he was at the grocery store when he caught a whiff of that unmistakable scent wafting from a bottle of hand sanitizer. Suddenly, his heart was racing, and his mind was flooded with images of his granddaughter's frail body hooked up to beeping machines. As a cybersecurity analyst, Kumar had always prided himself on being able to remain calm under pressure, but these physical reactions left him feeling helpless. The strong negative emotions that accompanied them – fear, horror, anger, guilt – made him question whether he was still the same man who had once been so in control. When his granddaughter's mother announced she was pregnant again a few months ago, Kumar felt like he'd been punched in the gut. He couldn't bear the thought of going through it all over again. Pregnancy and childbirth reminders sent him spiraling into memories of those torturous hospital visits. Those memories played on repeat in his mind like a film stuck on an endless loop. The sounds, sights, and smells came rushing back with such intensity that Kumar often felt as if he was reliving the experience right then and there. When his granddaughter finally went into remission, Kumar thought the worst was behind him, but the memories persisted, refusing to be relegated to the past. Even now, when people asked about that time, Kumar struggled to put it into words – his thoughts jumbled, and he'd lose track of what he wanted to say. The medical procedures themselves had been traumatic enough, but it was the aftermath – watching his family struggle to cope, feeling like he couldn't protect them from harm – that continued to haunt him. The triggers piled up: hospitals, babies, even certain smells. They brought back not only memories but also those suffocating feelings of helplessness and terror. Kumar felt trapped in a never-ending cycle where every reminder sparked another flashback, which in turn heightened his sense of threat. As the years passed, Kumar began to withdraw from social events, avoiding anything that might trigger these memories or reactions. His colleagues at work noticed the change but couldn't quite put their finger on what was wrong. He became more reclusive, shutting himself away with only his computers for company. The isolation suited him fine; it was a small price to pay for not having to face those memories head-on. Lately, though, even that seemed insufficient. Kumar's avoidance strategies weren't keeping the demons at bay as effectively as they used to. His granddaughter's upcoming fifth birthday party loomed on the horizon – a celebration that should have filled him with joy but now filled him with dread. As he grappled with whether to attend or make up an excuse, Kumar realized it was time to confront the memories and emotions he'd been running from for so long. He made an appointment with a therapist, hoping that finally facing his fears might help him break free from this suffocating cycle of pain and regret. Kumar sat in his armchair, staring out at the cityscape below, wondering what the future held – whether it would bring peace or more suffering. One thing was certain: he couldn't keep living like this, trapped by memories that refused to stay buried.
